lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: describe the structure of the thorax, including the ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and pleural membranes

primer.text: The thorax is a sealed chamber of bone, muscle and branching tubes. Air enters by one road — trachea, bronchi, bronchioles — and ends at the alveoli where exchange happens. Learn the parts, their order, and the shared adaptations that make the exchange fast.

modules.title: Inside the Thorax
modules.opening: The thorax is the chest cavity, holding the ribs, the intercostal muscles between them, the diaphragm below, and the respiratory tree: trachea to two bronchi, one per lung, branching into bronchioles that end in alveoli. Pleural membranes surround the lungs and line the cavity, and every structure plays its part in delivering air to the exchange surface.
keyPoints: The thorax contains ribs, intercostal muscles, the diaphragm, trachea, lungs and pleural membranes.
Inside the lungs the airway branches: bronchi, then bronchioles, then alveoli.
Ribs protect the organs; intercostal muscles move them for breathing.
The trachea connects mouth and nose to the lungs.
Pleural membranes surround the lungs and line the thorax.

low.restatement: One airway road, branching from wide to fine, ending at the alveoli.
low.analogy: A motorway becoming lanes becoming driveways, all ending at one big car park.
low.examPointer: Recite the air route in order — trachea, bronchus, bronchiole, alveolus — without mixing the middle two.

medium.restatement: Wide tube, two tubes, many tubes, sacs — the four levels of the airway.
medium.analogy: A river splitting into streams into rivulets into ponds.
medium.examPointer: Practise singular and plural forms; examiners mark the terms precisely.

modules.title: Shared Exchange Adaptations
modules.opening: Every exchange surface in biology shares the same toolbox, and the lungs show all of it: an enormous surface area from countless alveoli, walls one cell thick on both the alveolus and its capillary, ventilation that refreshes the air side, and a blood supply that renews the blood side. Together they hold the gradients steep and the distances short.
keyPoints: Many alveoli give the lungs a very large surface area.
Alveolus and capillary walls are one cell thick, minimising the diffusion distance.
Ventilation maintains a high oxygen and low carbon dioxide level in the alveolar air.
A good blood supply carries oxygenated blood away and carbon dioxide-rich blood in.
The same adaptations recur across all exchange surfaces.

low.restatement: Area, thinness, fresh air, fresh blood — the four-part recipe for fast exchange.
low.analogy: A market: huge floor space, low counters, constant restocking on both sides of every stall.
low.examPointer: List all four adaptations when a question asks how the lungs are suited to exchange.

medium.restatement: Both sides must stay imbalanced for exchange to stay fast.
medium.analogy: Two queues at a border, both kept short by frequent clearance.
medium.examPointer: Tie each adaptation to the word gradient — that is where the reasoning marks sit.

glossary.definition: The chest cavity containing the ribs, breathing muscles and airways.
Thin tissue layers surrounding the lungs and lining the thorax.
The thickness gas molecules must cross; kept minimal by one-cell-thick walls.
